tip: rester is a false friend: it means to stay, not to rest. Je reste à la maison = I stay home. To rest is se reposer.
avant de + infinitive = "before doing," when it's the same person doing both: avant de parler = before speaking.
Obéir needs à where English obeys directly: 'obéit à ses parents' is literally 'obeys to his parents'.
Entrer needs dans – you don't enter a place, you enter INTO it: 'entrez dans le magasin', never entrer le magasin.
Before a plural adjective, des shrinks to de: de bonnes vacances, not "des bonnes." Ils souhaitent de bonnes vacances = they wish happy holidays.
Object pronouns sit before the verb they act on: je peux vous aider = can I help you (literally "you help"). Never trailing after, as in English.
In speech a rising tone alone makes a question: 'Tu peux venir demain ?' keeps ordinary statement word order – no inversion required.
French builds noun compounds with de: un jus d'orange = an orange juice, "juice of orange." The describing noun comes second.
tous les + plural = "every": tous les matins = every morning (literally "all the mornings"). Also tous les jours = every day.
'Avoir besoin de' + infinitive = to need to. The 'de' links to the following verb.
Colours follow the noun in French: une voiture rouge = a red car, literally "a car red." Most descriptive adjectives come after.
French splits 'know' in two: connaître for people and places you're familiar with, savoir for facts. A doctor is someone you know, so 'je connais un bon médecin'.
Quantity words take de with no article: trop de café = too much coffee, beaucoup de = a lot of. The "some" article drops out.
Unsure whether to use tu or vous? Start with vous, as in 'Vous avez'. A wrong tu can offend; a wrong vous just sounds polite.
à + a time means "see you then": à demain = see you tomorrow, à bientôt = see you soon. À demain matin = see you tomorrow morning.

target: Vous rendez visite à vos parents.
tip: 'Rendre visite à' means 'to visit a person'. Don't confuse with 'visiter' which is for places: je visite le musée.

target: Je parle français tous les jours.
tip: After parler, the language drops its article: je parle français, not "le français." Compare j'apprends le français, which keeps it.

target: Où est l'hôpital le plus proche ?
tip: Superlatives use le/la plus + adjective: le plus proche = the nearest. The article repeats: l'hôpital le plus proche = the nearest hospital.
'Demander' means 'to ask for' – no extra preposition needed. 'Vous demandez l'addition' = You ask for the bill.
savoir + a verb = "know how to," with no word for "how": je sais nager = I can swim. pouvoir would mean you're merely allowed to.
'Je veux bien' is a polite way to accept an offer. It's softer than 'oui' and means 'yes, gladly' or 'I'd be happy to'.
Voyager is an -er verb ending in -ger. Add 'e' before -ons: nous voyageons, to keep the soft 'g' pronunciation.
attendre already means "to wait FOR" – no preposition follows: tu attends le bus = you wait for the bus, never "attends pour."

english: You try on this pair of pants.
tip: un pantalon is singular in French though "pants/trousers" is plural in English: ce pantalon = this one pair. Same with un jean.
To get off a vehicle is descendre de: ils descendent du train = they get off the train. Plain descendre alone just means "go down."
Months take en for "in": en juillet = in July, en mars = in March. Nous déménageons en juillet = we move house in July.
Récupérer looks like 'recuperate' but here means to collect or pick up: nous récupérons les valises = we get the suitcases back, not we recover from them.
allumer = switch on, éteindre = switch off (also to light or put out a fire): tu allumes la lumière = you turn on the light.
In French, age uses 'avoir' (to have): j'ai 20 ans = I am 20 years old. Literally 'I have 20 years'.
Au is à + le fused into one word: 'allez au marché' = go to the market. The two always merge.
